identification.title: Untitled Hymn (Come to Jesus)
identification.album: Run the Earth, Watch the Sky
identification.notes: Words and music by Chris Rice; copyright Clumsy Fly Music (administered by WC Music Corp.). The list's artist is right. The recording churches know is Rice's own on Run the Earth, Watch the Sky (2003, Rocketown Records); he re-recorded it for the 2019 collection Untitled Hymn: A Collection of Hymns. The reading note gave 1997, but the sources found in search results place the original at 2003, so 2003 is used here; search snippets only, no page for it was opened. No CCLI number was seen. Reviewed as the song, not any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Six short verses, each closing with a repeated threefold call to Jesus joined to a promise of life; the last closing call is sung twice. The voice is a pastoral address to the hearer: an invitation to the weak sinner, then cleansing and a lifted burden, then grace for the one who falls, then crying out in lonely and painful times, then overflowing joy, then a peaceful death that enters glory. Each stanza names a posture (come, sing, fall, cry, dance, fly). Christ is named throughout as the one to whom the hearer comes, and the cleansing is tied to his blood in the second verse. Nothing is said of the incarnation, the resurrection as event, the Spirit or the church.

claims.claim: Weary sinners are invited to come to Jesus, and life is promised to those who come.
claims.subject: Invitation of the gospel

claims.claim: Jesus's blood cleanses the sinner and lifts the burden of guilt.
claims.subject: Cleansing by the blood

claims.claim: Grace meets the believer who falls, and the fall is not the end.
claims.subject: Grace for the failing

claims.claim: In lonely and painful seasons the believer may cry out to Jesus and be heard.
claims.subject: Prayer in suffering

claims.claim: Joy in Christ may overflow into praise and rejoicing.
claims.subject: Joy

claims.claim: A believer's death is peaceful and enters the presence of Christ in glory.
claims.subject: Death and glory

strengths.title: The open call of Christ
strengths.explanation: Each verse comes back to Christ's open invitation and the promise of life, so the whole song sounds like the gospel call to the weary rather than a report of the singer's feelings.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Christ calls the weary and burdened to come to him; the song's repeated call builds on this.

strengths.title: Cleansing by Christ's blood
strengths.explanation: The second verse ties the lifted burden to the blood that washes the sinner, placing forgiveness in what Christ has done and not in the hearer's effort.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The blood of Jesus purifies from all sin; the verse rests the cleansing there.

strengths.title: Grace for the one who falls
strengths.explanation: The song speaks to the believer who stumbles and answers with grace, which keeps assurance from resting on performance.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The free invitation to come and live; the song echoes its logic of grace without price.

strengths.title: Death met with Christ, not dread
strengths.explanation: The last verse sets a believer's death as peaceful entry into glory with Christ, a plain and pastoral statement of the Christian hope.
strengths.scriptureRationale: To depart and be with Christ is far better; the verse matches the hope Paul states.

doctrinesAffirmed: The free invitation of the gospel
Cleansing by the blood of Christ
Grace toward the believer who falls
Being with Christ in glory after death
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. The note flags that the life promised after each call to sing, dance and rest might sound like conditions for life. Read in the song's order it does not: the invitation and the cleansing by Christ's blood come first, and the later postures are the believer's response to a life already given. The gospel is implicit rather than fully stated; the cross is reached only through the blood, and the resurrection is not.

strengths.title: A closing call anyone can join
strengths.explanation: Every verse ends on a short repeated call, so a congregation can join by the second verse without a sheet. The folk-like tune is gentle and sits comfortably as a sung prayer.

strengths.title: One song for many conditions
strengths.explanation: The stanzas run from guilt through grief to joy and death, so a room of mixed circumstances finds its own condition in it.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published keys were not checked. The tune is folk-like and moderate; test a key where the closing call sits comfortably for untrained voices and keep the accompaniment sparse.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: Each verse closes on the same repeated call to Jesus, and the final one is sung twice. The repeat returns to the invitation each time, so it carries the song's point rather than filling space.
communal.assessment: Congregational in words and shape: a pastoral address with short, repeating, easily joined closings. It suits communion, times of weariness or grief, funerals, and services of invitation.

strengths.title: Jesus is the one addressed
strengths.explanation: Jesus is named in the closing call of every verse, so the hearer always knows to whom the invitation points.

clarity.assessment: Plain and clear. The images are biblical and easily understood. The one point a leader may want to explain is that the singing, falling, crying and dancing are the believer's response to the invitation, not the price of life.

synthesis.summary: A six-verse pastoral invitation to come to Jesus, moving from the weary sinner through cleansing by his blood, grace for the one who falls, suffering, joy, and a peaceful death into glory. Each verse closes on the same call and a promise of life. The promise could be misheard as conditional, but the gospel frame of the second verse answers that. The cross and resurrection are only implicit.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Christ's call to the weary and burdened; the frame of the song's repeated call.
The free invitation to come and live.
The blood of Jesus cleansing from sin; behind the second verse.
Weeping for a night and joy in the morning; behind the verses on pain and joy.
Departing to be with Christ; behind the last verse.
